items.scene: A worker checks 10 boxes from a shipment of 100 and finds 7 damaged.
items.question: What should she estimate about the whole shipment?
items.why_this_case_matters: A small observed sample should revise the estimate for the larger unseen set.

items.scene: A manager says, "Most of the cafe's cups are usually clean." No cups have been checked today.
items.question: What should she conclude about today's cups?
options: They must almost all be clean
The phrase is only a general expectation; she still needs actual observation
The phrase alone gives a precise count
items.why_this_case_matters: This is about a vague prior, not a new sample-based update.

items.scene: A company usually ships reliable products. Today, nobody has opened any boxes yet, but someone asks how many are likely damaged.
items.question: Which factor should mainly drive the estimate?
options: Who would be blamed if there is a complaint
The exact wording of the question
items.why_this_case_matters: This relies on a background base rate, not on a newly observed sample.

items.scene: A teacher asks three students sitting in the front row whether they finished homework, and all three say yes.
items.question: Should she now think almost everyone finished?
options: No, the sample is tiny and possibly biased, so the estimate should rise only a little
Yes, because three yes answers prove the whole class did it
No, the answers prove nobody else finished
items.why_this_case_matters: This uses partial observation, but the sample is small and biased, so the update should be weak.
